title: Choose CampusNav's new visual world
question: I translated the building's real navigation task into several complete interface systems. Choose one, or re-roll the hand.

options.label: Field Trace
options.lineage: architectural field plans, survey notes, and drawing-set tabs
options.thesis: CampusNav becomes the working route sheet carried through the building: the map is the surface, the route is the live annotation, and every confirmed point is a field mark.
options.viewport: A large live floor plan owns the screen; a slim indexed planning strip sits left, oversized floor tabs bind the right edge, and the next instruction is stamped into the bottom of the drawing.
options.risk: It can feel like sterile CAD if room names and physical actions are allowed to shrink into technical notation.

raised.raise: Primary actions gain unmistakable tactile hierarchy and a single commit color.
Cross-floor progress gains one disciplined vertical axis rather than scattered floor status.
The route line visibly changes the whole interface state instead of acting as decoration.
Unavailable connectors use a pattern and mark, never color alone.

options.label: Corridor Bands
options.lineage: painted campus wayfinding bands, room plaques, and directory pylons
options.thesis: The digital interface behaves like the best physical wayfinding system the building could have had, carrying one colored route band from search to arrival.
options.viewport: A bold route band physically connects the planner, the active map, the floor number, and the next-action dock as one uninterrupted navigation cue.
options.risk: This is the most immediately familiar direction and can become ordinary transit UI if the band stops governing the composition.

options.label: Route Console
options.thesis: Planning a route feels like setting a dependable instrument: two physical input bays, one mode bank, one decisive orange action, and a focused live status display.
options.viewport: A compact control deck occupies the lower-left corner of a dominant map, with each floor rendered as a whole key unit and route state reported on one amber display.
options.case: Matches the need for certainty and fast operation, but students identify less naturally with studio hardware than with campus artifacts.
options.risk: Too many tactile details could compete with the map at small sizes.

options.label: Checkpoint Rail
options.lineage: film cutting bench and perforated select rail
options.thesis: Every checkpoint is a physical frame on one route strip; the confirmed point carries a folded flag and no skipped step disappears.
options.viewport: The live map sits above a horizontal checkpoint rail whose frames snap forward one physical step at a time, with deferred or blocked connectors pinned below.
options.case: Manual checkpoint confirmation maps perfectly to the system, but the dark orange field is less comfortable in bright corridors and during long map reading.
options.risk: The cinematic metaphor may be more memorable than the building itself.

options.label: Modular Campus
options.lineage: hard vector bars and modular identity blocks
options.thesis: Floors and facilities snap into a bold identity grid around the map.
options.viewport: Color blocks frame the floor plan and move forward as floors or facilities become active.
options.case: The energy suits campus life, but dense colors obscure route state and semantic facility colors.
options.kept: A strict modular grid now keeps Field Trace from drifting into loose dashboard panels.
options.risk: The identity can overpower the map's required semantic palette.

options.label: Floor Descent
options.thesis: An eight-level depth axis turns every floor change into one continuous vertical journey.
options.viewport: A vertical floor profile rules the composition beside a dark map field and highlights the current level as a cyan thermocline.
options.case: The floor model is legible, but a dark immersive environment performs poorly for an everyday campus tool in varied light.
options.kept: Field Trace adopts one continuous vertical floor axis with an unmistakable current-level marker.
options.risk: Immersion would reduce long-session map readability and print-like spatial clarity.

options.label: Route Tension
options.thesis: One continuous route line gathers the interface from planning into navigation.
options.viewport: The selected route pulls panels and floor states into a single shaped silhouette around the live map.
options.case: The state transformation is powerful, but the fashion grammar does not help students understand rooms or controls.
options.kept: The chosen route now visibly reorganizes the entire surface from planning mode to guidance mode.
options.risk: Its beautiful transformation would demand too much explanation.

options.label: Route Exposure
options.lineage: darkroom exposure record and translucent zone sheets
options.thesis: Routes, facilities, and blocked connectors occupy measured translucent layers over the authoritative floor plan.
options.viewport: A pale plan is layered with a single translucent route sheet and a compact record of distance, floor, and next action.
options.case: Overlays fit the map, but photographic notation is unfamiliar and too abstract for urgent wayfinding.
options.kept: Blocked and completed route states gain pattern-level encoding that remains clear without color.
options.risk: Layering could make the already detailed SVG feel visually muddy.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A polished conventional map app: a white route form beside a familiar blue indoor map.
canonCard.viewport: A left sidebar handles origin and destination while the floor plan fills the remaining space with familiar floating map controls.
canonCard.risk: Immediately usable, deliberately indistinguishable from other navigation products.
